title: Great Effort
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and awareness through rigorous training and discipline, but not in a way that seeks to suppress or overcome one's natural tendencies. Instead, it encourages embracing and sitting with difficult emotions and thoughts, such as hazing and self-concern, directly and without resistance, allowing for greater ease and clarity in daily life. By approaching practice with kindness, self-awareness, and mindfulness, individuals can develop a strong foundation for spiritual growth and awakening.

sentences.text: Nice to see you here, old friends and new, at the retreat and just coming for the talk.
I actually couldn't give the talk if you weren't here.
It's true.
I really couldn't do it.
*The usual day at Dai Tokuji monastery begins at 3 a.m. with the ring of a handbell and a voice shouting, "Kaijo, get up."
The monks jump out of bed and pour from a small bamboo dipper onto their palms the three scoops of water that they are allotted to rinse their mouths and wash their face.
Then they go to the toilet, put on their robes and present themselves in the main Buddha hall.
Each action of every person is orchestrated so that the group works together as a whole.
When the gong sounds in the main hall signaling the monks to appear, the leader of the zendo, the ino, rings his small bell and everyone files out in silence.
And then the morning sutra chanting in the main hall lasts for about an hour.*
So that's two different buildings: a building that they sleep in and do meditation in, and a different building for the service.
And so we do sutra chanting for about an hour at four in the morning.
Sutra chanting is one activity that affords me countless opportunities to meet my mistakes head on.
*After the morning chanting the monks return to the zendo and then the zazen period begins.
At the clang of the special bell they set out for sanzen, the private meeting with the teacher.* We call it dokusan.
They call it sanzen in this system.
*One by one they go in to encounter the teacher face to face.
What takes place now is not a convivial meeting between equals but a very pointed question and answer session.
Each monk has received from his teacher a koan which he must answer at this private meeting.
The monk must master the true meaning of the koan through earnest zazen, not mere cogitation and worry.
When the sanzen period is finished is breakfast time.
For the first four years that I lived in the monastery the food we ate did not appear to be food at all.
Gradually the diet did move towards what we would now call traditional.
But then our gruel consisted of round unprocessed barley, not the pressure steamed and dried barley used in cooking today.*
Maybe you're not used to eating barley in the morning at all, but early days here, unprocessed barley.
*Gruel is so much the standard morning fare in Zen monasteries that the very word for breakfast is derived from this dish.
Regardless of how long unprocessed barley is boiled it does not thicken the water, so the end result amounts to nothing more than salty water in which grains of barley have settled to the bottom.
Along with this gruel for about three years we were served nothing more but two smelly [unclear: "barackish"] slices of what we called perpetual pickles.
We would carefully suck the saltiness out of these two pickles as we ate, or should I say drank, our three bowls of gruel.
It's often said the Zen monks eat pickles without making a sound, but the truth is that the pickles we had to chew weren't crunchy anyway.
Don't be too impressed by their quiet pickle chewing.
No matter how frugally and gingerly one licks at each pickle to try to make it last, before you know it the pickle is gone and dissolved and slid down the throat.

And this is indeed the case not only with eating pickles but with every movement in the dining hall: the raising and lowering of the chopsticks, the picking up and setting down of the bowl, sipping on the hot gruel.
Absolutely no sound is allowed and no sound is made.
Whispering is out of the question.
All action is orchestrated with designated gestures and the sound of wooden clappers.*
*The dining hall, along with the bath and the toilet building, are known as the three halls of silence where quiet is strictly enforced.
It goes without saying of course that silence is always maintained in the meditation hall, a real silence.
All the fledgling monks reside together 24 hours a day, each in his assigned place on one tatami mat in the hall with no partitions, and there is no such thing as private time or private space.
Consequently the only occasion one is completely alone is in the toilet, and so they require the monks remain silent even there, probably the only way to continue being mindful.*
*Bath day in the monastery occurs on every date of the month that ends in a four or a nine, so the fourth, the ninth, the fourteenth and so on.
The monks not only take baths on this day but they wash their clothes, mend their robes and kimono and take care of any personal affairs that have arisen.
At any rate they get a bath only once every five days.

No matter who a person is, if one arises at three in the morning and goes to bed late doing zazen and manual labor day in and day out, the pleasure of stepping into a hot bath is like an ascent to heaven.
One's spirits rise to exhilaration despite oneself.
For this reason the bath is also one of the three halls of silence.*
Let us return to the dining hall.
*It's important that the quiet be the rule here because regardless of how poor one's food is, it is easy for a monk to allow his mind to wander.
Indeed I might even say that the poorer the fare, the more likely the mind is to wander, in my experience.
After breakfast the monks clean inside and outside the hall before setting out just after seven a.m. on their begging rounds.

Days for begging alternate with days in which the master gives a talk, so that if the talk is given on the second, fifth, seventh and tenth of the month, then the first, third, sixth and eighth of the month will be begging days.*
As there are seven training halls in Kyoto, this schedule is set up so that monks from neighboring monasteries will not go out and beg on the same day, to not overwhelm the neighborhood.
*When monks return from begging at about 10 a.m. it's time for lunch.
This meal consists of barley rice, miso soup with a few greens, and two more pickles.
Approximately one part rice is added to nine parts unprocessed barley.* Calling it rice is a stretch.

*After this mixture is boiled to the softest possible consistency it is mashed with a ladle so that the crushed barley becomes at least a little bit sticky. [unclear: "Unmasked"] the barley will remain crunchy and be quite inedible.
For supper the leftovers from lunch are thrown together to form a kind of hodgepodge.
When the monks eat too much barley rice at lunch there's not enough left.
Extra water is added to the hodgepodge at supper, making an especially watery concoction.
That is our dinner.*
I don't know what word in Japanese that was, but hodgepodge.
*Lunch is followed by a period of manual labor called samu.
Tasks here might include working in the monastery vegetable garden, pruning shrubs and trees, pulling weeds and splitting firewood.
Work is given special emphasis in monastic life, and the monks are constantly cautioned not to consider the weight of a job in relative terms.* So one job is not more important than another job.
*But to drop all analysis and apply themselves wholeheartedly to the task at hand until it's time to stop.*
*After the work period and this medicinal supper of hodgepodge,* the word for supper, literally written, means "medicine stone."
The two characters are "medicine stone," so just like stone soup we have in English, like stone soup.
*Then the monks enter the zendo and do zazen again until 9 p.m.
During this period they have another sanzen encounter with the master, the second of the day.
At 9 p.m. special sutras are read before bedtime, and "bedtime" here is written in quotes.
The literal meaning of bedtime here is to lift the rules.
This does not mean though that the rules are lifted.
When the sutra is finished and the lights go out everyone does not go right to sleep.*
Here's how it works.

*Once the sutra is chanted,* so this is like 9:30 or something, *the monk in charge rings his bell, the monks quickly take off their robes, take their bedding down from their shelf and fall into an orderly line into bed, for the time being that is.
You may never have a chance to see the inside of a zendo, we would call [unclear: "asodo"], monk's hall, but you can picture this by imagining an army barracks.*
I've heard it said that when the [unclear: "zensek"] decided to build a [unclear: "asodo"] they looked to the army barracks for their example.

*There's one long row of tatami mats on each side of the hall on a raised platform, and each monk is allowed a single mat for everything: zazen, sleeping, and conducting his life.* And you get a little shelf at the end.
*The aisle between the two rows of mats is covered with Japanese style tiles.
Bedding consists of a single futon just folded in half and serves as both the mattress and the cover.
This is referred to as the oak leaf futon because the monk fits inside the futon like a sweet bean rice cake that is usually wrapped in a single oak leaf.
The monk who is accustomed to this bedding can skillfully wrap himself in, like a rolled sea tangle, and be quite warm.
At any rate summer or winter this one layer is the monk's only bedding.

Just as soon as the monk in charge of the zendo, carrying his stick called the kesaku, the reminder stick, has finished his inspection of the long rows of rolled sea tangle monks, the lights are switched off, the senior monks leave the zendo.

This is the cue for the others to get out of bed, quickly put their robes back on, and carrying their zazen mats under their arms head outside to find a place under the eaves of the main hall or in the graveyard, each to his own choice, to continue with nighttime sitting.
I myself used to choose the tombstone with the highest base I could for nighttime sitting.
I had in all sincerity come up with the childish notion that perching on top of a high stone, a dangerous place to doze off, would prevent me from getting drowsy.*
He doesn't comment on whether, I guess he survived, and say whether he ever fell off.
*And so how it works is until nine o'clock everyone sits together in the zendo, and then after the rules are lifted everyone voluntarily sits on his own.
For the monk new to life in the dojo, customs of this sort are nothing but arduous.
It gradually dawned on me though that the practice of night sitting makes sense.*
This is relevant.
We're going to maybe do some night sitting in our retreat here, so let's hear what he has to say.
Why would this make sense?
*Just as everyone is endowed with his own particular facial features, so each person's situation is uniquely his or her own, making for a countless variety of circumstances.
The heart with which one is born is a wonderful thing, but the after effects of accumulated experiences and knowledge vary with each person.
For this reason time is set aside for individual sitting after the lights go out.*
That's his explanation: because they're all different, we need to do this extra sitting.
*In the order of their seniority the monks finally return to the zendo to sleep.
This means the most junior of the monks go last and do not get to bed until a little bit after midnight.
It follows then that on regular days they clock in about three hours of sleep.
Weakling that I was, I always had the feel of just fainting rather than falling asleep.
What's more, during one week of the month devoted to intensive zazen called sesshin, sleep is even less.
So to describe these zendo customs may paint a picture of an insanely severe lifestyle.*
Did you think that?
*But during the period of life when one is flush with energy and vigor it's impossible to really settle into quiet zazen practice if one sleeps too much, and by the same token if one eats too much.
So following a plain vegetarian diet and a strong schedule helps the mind to some degree, and I believe this is necessary.
In the zendo lifestyle private ownership is strictly limited too.
Monks carry out their lives on the barest necessities: a loin cloth, a thin cotton undergarment, a wide belt, a kimono and a light outer robe, even in wintertime.
There's no thicker or lined kimono.*
He goes on about that for a bit.
*To be frank though, after a year or so most monks become accustomed to this rigorous monastery life.
You get used to it and the physical rigors cease to become of much consequence.
But the most distressing aspect of training is not the physical suffering but the spiritual agony that invariably accompanies these private dialogues with the teacher.
This distress decidedly does not disappear after a year.
The heart of the encounter with the teacher is the student's presentation of a koan.*
For illustration I'll use one of the most famous koans.
Show your original face before the birth of your mother and father.
Just show your original face.
This koan asks, in other words, what is your true form?

*Some of you will submit that this question is ridiculous, but the monk who was given this koan knows that he must without fail take a solution into his teacher the following morning, and he is compelled to work on it as if for dear life.
Going at it with desperation, the first thing he realizes is that while the physical body is passed on from parent to child, life itself continues infinitely.
No child is born after the parent's death. [unclear: "Fascinating"] by the death of the physical body we make all these divisions: the life of the parent, the life of the child, my life, your life.
But in reality, even if we endlessly retrace the past, the life that we're living now is infinite, and we cannot pin down any beginnings to it.
We can understand this much through simple reasoning.*
Maybe, but he's saying this is the result of studying this koan.
You get a different view of life and death.
*Furthermore, the great functioning of this life is the functioning of the mind.
To think of it in purely logical terms, the question arises, transcending this thing called myself: What is life?
What is it that continues?* And so it goes on about that a bit.
*How much they could learn from these [unclear: "odds"] and koans, and the pressure to work with them constantly.
This private interview with the teacher takes place two or three times each day, morning and evening, on regular days, and three times a day during intensive periods.*
*Additionally, there is an especially intensive period called Rohatsu sesshin.
This is held once a year from December 1st through the 8th.
This week of practice commemorates the great enlightenment that Shakyamuni Buddha experienced upon seeing the morning star on December the 8th.
During this week no one may lie down to sleep, and there are four private meetings with the teacher every day.
No amount of theorizing will help the monk pass his koan in these situations. [unclear: "No fear he is involved"].
When all reasoning is exhausted and the bell is rung to call the monks yet again to meet the roshi, he finds that he cannot leave his zazen mat.* The guy got stupefied or something.
*He can't move.
On regular days the monk might be permitted to forego the meeting and continue zazen.
But during the week of sesshin practice, however, two or three senior monks with faces like the devil will come.
They will jerk the unwilling monk off his cushion and encourage him to go to the teacher.
The monk cannot avoid this meeting just because he has no answer to the koan or doesn't know what to say.
If one looks at the pillars between the zendo and the interview room, one finds numerous scratches.* I'll skip the explanation why the scratches are there.
You probably figured it out.
*The monk finds himself before the roshi, silent, without an answer.
He can expect the roshi to bellow, "What are you doing here?"
And to strike him with his thick stick, clobbered from all sides, the monk knows that even if he makes it through this one there will be another mandatory meeting face to face a few hours later.
No matter how [unclear: "lazier cunning"] the monk may be, he is driven into a corner, and he cannot contrive to wriggle his way through with half-hearted or makeshift answers.*
I should mention this style of training is particularly found in the monasteries of the Rinzai sect, as opposed to the [unclear: "sotos and"] monasteries, so don't worry.
That's what he said, that was his words.
*As a [unclear: "relative's"] experience living this way and studying koans, I often dreamed I would have satori.

I'd have awakening when I was in the training hall, and I dreamed that upon awakening I would find that for the most part* — oh, and "upon away," I think it means when you wake up in the morning, and waking up in the morning — *I would find in the most part that this direct realization was trifling and not real.

There are times, however, when the experience I had in a dream held up even when I woke up.* In other words, after a while I couldn't tell really, you know, whether you're awake or asleep, dreaming or not.
*Two or three times I had this experience, and I went in high spirits to meet my teacher, and I did pass my koan.*
*Every night I finally got the opportunity to roll myself up again in my oak leaf style futon.
Rather than falling asleep I would fall into a sort of unconsciousness, and within an instant I'd be roused to start another day.
Yet each time I fell into this swoon of sleep, the last thing to stay awake was the koan.
The first thing to wake up was the koan.
The body [unclear: "speaks"] but the mind continues to meet the teacher and meet the koan.
The sense of inquiry persisting, original face, original face, takes over even dreams.
And then every morning comes the monk running through the zendo clanging the bell and shouting, "Get up!
Get up!"
When one awakens, that sound, even before one is fully conscious, this sense of question, original face, is there in action.
Awareness of a problem awakens first, and consciousness comes around at length.
Incredible though it may seem, this was my experience in training at Daitokuji Monastery.*
So here we have an example from the late 1940s, maybe the early 1950s, of the Japanese style of hard training.
This was indeed from the Rinzai school, but we have similar traditions in the Soto school, actually, in the training monasteries in Japan.
This is from the autobiography of a man named Soko Morinaga.
He was born in 1925 and was a young soldier in the war, but he doesn't really comment on that beyond saying that he survived.
After the war he didn't really know what to do with his life, so he went into Zen training.
So he's a little bit unusual: he wasn't in a temple family, and he chose to go into this.
In this monastery where he was, Daitokuji, I got to visit.
It's still there, you can visit it.
I didn't get to see the monks hall, that's private to the monks in training, but you get to see quite a bit of it.
This was also the same place in Kyoto where Gary Snyder and other Americans, pioneers, did Zen practice, the first people from our culture to try this style of training.
It would have been much like described by Morinaga Hiroshi, although I think most of those guys didn't actually live there; they'd go home at night.
I remember there's a story of Gary Snyder, a little motorbike, take off, you know, at midnight through the streets of Kyoto, and sleep for a few hours in his apartment and go back.
So, hard training: part of the thought is to loosen us up to work in a very experiential way with self-concern, with comfort needs, right?
Obviously no comfort needs really can survive that onslaught.
One would not live that way one's whole life, so it's different from some other Buddhist traditions where the monastics live in a certain way their whole life.
This is a period of intensive training for a few years.
I think Morinaga Hiroshi was a little bit longer than usual, five or six years, and usually it's done as a young man.
There are also nuns in Japan, women monastics, but it's a much smaller movement, and I don't know that much about their training, but I'm sure it's also intense.
And the Buddha himself did a period of hard training, his famous six years of ascetic practice, also as a young man.
So since we're celebrating the Buddha this weekend with a little bit of our style of hard practice, I thought it'd be nice to remember a little bit about the Buddha's experience of hard practice.
The Buddha was just really sort of following the best practices of the day.

The thought amongst the wandering ascetics and monastic practitioners when he left home was that the way we cling to sensory desire and pleasure is a big, big part of the problem, a big source of suffering.
So, not unlike the Christian ascetics, they wanted to just cut that off, cut it off at the root, with experiential work.

So after studying with a few teachers and actually having very deep meditation experiences, the Buddha-to-be heads off into the forest with a couple of buddies, a couple of Dharma buddies, to do these ascetic practices, not as structured as Morinaga Roshi's experience but similar in style.
Here we have from the earliest text, supposedly, the Buddha's own words describing how he practiced during that period.
I thought: think about how to work with his mind, like his mind is probably wandering, right?
Have you thought about this?
How do I work with his mind that's wandering?
Here's how he thought to work with his mind, to stop this kind of wandering mind, the proliferation of mind, right.
*Suppose I were to clench my teeth, press my tongue against the roof of my mouth, beat down, constrain and crush my mind with awareness.* You ever try this?

*Clenching my teeth and pressing my tongue against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained and crushed my mind with my awareness.* Now what's interesting here is the Buddha is by now a very skilled meditator and has been training for a long time, full time, you know, and he started out, due to past, you know, previous life experiences in this model, already with lots and lots of experience.
So he's like the best meditator in the world, practically, right, at this point, and so he has a lot of mental skills, meditative skills and faculties.
So he can actually do this: he can crush his mind with his mind, successfully.
*So I did this.
I crushed my mind with my awareness.
It felt just like a strong man seizing a weaker man by the head or the throat or the shoulders, and the strong man beat him down, constrained him and crushed him.
In the same way I beat down, constrained and crushed my mind with my awareness.
And as I did so, sweat poured from my armpits, and although tireless persistence was aroused in me.* So that's interesting.
It didn't freak him out, actually.
Like, okay, I can do this, I can be present in the middle of crushing my own mind, incredible pain, right?
He was energized by this.
*So even though tireless persistence was aroused in me and unmuddled mindfulness established.* His concentration was really good, and sometimes pain does have that quality.
If you're in pain it's sometimes possible to be very concentrated, really aware of what's happening now.
*So my mindfulness was established, but my body was aroused and [unclear: "uncalled"] because of this painful exertion, but still that painful feeling did not invade my mind or remain.*
So it's interesting, what he's saying: he could do this incredibly difficult thing to himself and stay very present and not freak out.
He goes on, he tries a whole series of things like that.
He tries not-breathing practice, he tries not-eating practice, and at one point the people around, and the gods kind of watching from above, aren't even sure if he's still alive.
They have, like, a little discussion: is he still alive down there?
Like, no, I think he's barely alive, they decide.
And finally he does eat a little bit, and he goes on like this for quite a long time.

But then he realizes, bottom line, the suffering is still there, you know, this sense, the sense that things are not quite what we like, the sense of disease and dissatisfaction, the heart not being at rest.
He could notice that even though he had this incredible concentration and he could do these really hard practices, it kind of didn't help the root problem that he set out to work on.
And so finally he decides to ease up a little bit.
It's not clear in the account what led him to realize he should just, you know, ease up a little bit.
Maybe six years was enough.
Probably we wouldn't have lasted quite six years.
And when he decides to ease up a little bit, something internally shifts, some subtle shift happens that has a big effect.
Then, to this day for us, when he decides to ease up a little bit, he decides to eat a little bit, somehow this wonderful girl from the village just happens to come along with some food.
This always happens in the stories, right?
This one is going to be a great, beautiful young girl, and it was rice pudding.
It's one thing you could maybe even eat if you've been eating a grain of rice for a year, or six years: some really soft rice pudding.
So he eats the rice pudding and he sits down, and then a memory comes to him, a really pivotal memory.
This is his account of remembering that memory:
*The thought came to me.
I remembered*
*I remembered when I was seven years old, when my father the* [unclear: "sock in"] *was busy, while sitting in the cool shade of a tree.*
According to the commentary he was seven years old.
The back story they give in the commentary is that it was the springtime and they're having a special ceremony to mark the first plowing of the fields, or whatever time it is in India.
The rains had ended, and it was one of the first times that the young prince had been left alone.
So he's sitting off to the side under a tree while his father's doing this ceremony with the village.

*My father the* [unclear: "sock in"] *was busy and I was sitting in the cool shade of a tree, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, just sitting there secluded from unskillful states, and I remembered that I entered into and abided in the first state of concentration, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and joy and happiness born out of seclusion.*
So he just remembered, as a child, this moment of just peaceful joy, this moment of things just being fine.
Can you remember a moment like that?
It's not so much the external circumstances, but somehow there's this moment when things are just clear, just beautiful.
Maybe it lasts for a second or a minute or an hour, but that's sort of just resting in awareness, resting in experience.
So here he is, after having nearly killed himself with ascetic practices, and he remembered that feeling from childhood.
Then, this is him later:
*Maybe this is the path to awakening.
Following that memory came the consciousness: this is the path to awakening.*
So it just came to him: there's something in that feeling.
And then the question came:
*Why am I afraid of happiness that is not connected to sensual pleasures, that is not connected to unskillful states?*
*And then a thought came to me: I should not be afraid of this happiness, for this happiness is born of freedom, not bound up in sensual pleasures and unskillful states.*
From there the story unfolded.

He sat down under the tree and had whatever experience or experiences that we now call awakening or enlightenment, some deep sense of the nature of reality and the nature of being that empowered him in some way to shift his view and to shift the views of the people he worked with.

There are many wonderful stories in the early writings of it going both ways: meeting somebody in a short conversation with the Buddha, and it just somehow really helps somebody to shift their view and see their life in a fresh way that inclines them towards liberation from suffering and self-concern.
Then, also importantly for us, there are stories where it doesn't happen, too.
Just to mention that, the best one is the first person he meets.

I didn't bring the story, but just to summarize it: the first person he meets after this great experience of awakening, and after hanging out for a while in this peaceful abiding experience for some time, and finally deciding, well, maybe he could explain this.
At first he thought, "Nobody's going to understand this.
I wouldn't have understood it myself.
Nobody's gonna understand this freedom.
They're all too caught."
So at first he was just going to bliss out for the remaining years until the body stopped working, and that would be that.
Then he decided to go teach, and the first person he runs into is a merchant or somebody walking down the road.
The Buddha comes running up proclaiming his great understanding, and the guy says, "Oh, is that so?" and leaves.
You can imagine.
Have you met people like that?
"Oh, I've got this great thing, I'm telling you about this wonderful thing, this great new diet, whatever it is.
It will definitely make you happy.
You'll clear up that problem you're having, absolutely."
Somebody is a little bit like that, and I'm like, "Oh yeah, that's nice."
But eventually, of course, he did go on to teach and have many, many students, and they went on themselves to study and practice and teach.
And then somehow, 2,500 years later, here we are, celebrating the Buddha's enlightenment.
But it's interesting about the periods of hard training in the Buddha story and in Morinaga's story that I read you.
I thought you'd also like to hear a little bit about what this might look like in Japan, a little different than the way we do it, maybe you noticed.
Morinaga Roshi didn't even talk about the style of instruction, probably because he takes it for granted that that's how instructions are always given: usually very brusque.
The usual system is, "Do this job," and they don't tell you how to do it, and you fumble around and then they come right behind you and say, "Not that way," right?
So here in our cultural milieu, the senior people [unclear: "even look at anybody funny"], it's like a big crisis, and we have to have conflict resolution meetings, right?
Which is fine.
We need to learn how to be kind and how to resolve our conflicts and honor each other and all this.
That's our cultural meme in our way of practicing, and there's nothing wrong with that.
But yeah, a little different system there.
There was none of that: you don't like it, you leave.
So what about this hard training?
Now, I never met Morinaga Roshi, but his autobiography is called *Novice to Master: An Ongoing Lesson in the Extent of My Own Stupidity*.
That's the title.
There's a kind of Japanese style of humility in the title, acknowledging your own stupidity, right?
We would go to a psychologist for self-empowerment if we had that attitude.
Our self-image needs to be worked on anyway.

And yet in his book he comes off as just very kind, grandfatherly is how he really comes off, like he really was a loving, kind person with his students once he finished his training and went on to be a teacher himself.
Willing to be clear with people, not fuzzy, willing to call things the way he saw them, it seems.
He describes some encounters he has with students, but very kind, very grounded, sweet man.
And the Buddha too comes off that way in the early writings: very clear with people, directive when he needs to be, but with a real feeling of a loving heart.
You can really tell, even thousands of years later, in translation, third hand, that the Buddha was very grounding and very loving.
So do we need this hard practice, or is hard practice just a mistake that these guys had to go through?
If only the Buddha had known, if you'd remember that memory one year in [unclear: "may"] you could save himself a lot of trouble, right?
Five years of pain.
Maybe if the Japanese monastic system received modern pedagogical training from the best minds in Western education, they could drop all this ego-crushing, mean hazing.
And I didn't read you what he had to do to get admitted to the monastery.
It's a little bit frightening, actually.
Or is somehow working hard in our practice an ingredient that we all need?

How do we work with this self that's always bubbling up, this self-concern that wants reassurance, that wants everybody to like us, the self who has a happiness that's contingent on circumstances being just the right way?
How do we work with this self?
Do we need to batter it with tough, strong training?
Do we need to just sit in the middle of it and see it for what it is?
Hearing these stories, it's also, I think, pretty easy for us to distance ourselves from them.
We can say, "Well, that's another culture, that's not our culture," as I just did.
In fact, we could say, "That's for young people, I'm too old."
We could say, "That's for men, I'm not male."
We could say, "That was a long time ago," in the case of the Buddha, "now we know better."
It's really hard to know.
I don't have an answer.
